summary:
A Charter newsletter item combining AI labor-market data points with a Q&A with American Federation of Teachers president Randi Weingarten about AI in schools.

AI and Work Radar highlights: LinkedIn analysis of roughly 15,000 companies across 27 countries found women were only 26% of US AI hires in 2025 versus 50% of hires in non-AI occupations, and hold 20% of head of AI roles, 18% of member of technical staff titles, and 13% of C-suite AI roles at AI companies globally. Pew Research Center data shows a majority of young adults are now more concerned than excited about AI, with the sharpest rise in concern among under-30s and declining concern among those 50 to 64. Bridgewater internal analysis suggests 18% of US jobs could be displaced within five years, with leaders proposing early policy action such as a tax on AI tokens. Goldman Sachs research finds AI already denting hiring in developed economies, most notably in software publishing, consulting, advertising, and call centers. A General Assembly survey says nearly half of leaders factor AI usage into performance evaluations; Gusto labels workers with one of five archetypes in quarterly reviews, and Travelport built a manager dashboard showing whether engineers use certain AI features.

Weingarten argues the labor movement is at a precipice: union approval near 70% while density sits at 10%, and AFT has grown to 1.875 million members. She called for banning student-facing AI tools for elementary students while investing in active learning, warning that early AI use offloads learning and erodes attention, cognition, and persistence, comparing it to screen-time bans at districts including LAUSD. Key skills for an AI economy: critical thinking, communication, persistence, and relational skills, plus AI fluency by junior high. AFT launched the National Academy for AI Instruction, training about 14,000 teachers last year.
